items.title: EvoSafeHarness: Evolving Model- and Domain-Specific Harnesses for Securing Agents
items.text:
Large Language Model (LLM) agents are turning language into real-world effects, making safety necessary against both indirect prompt injections and direct harmful requests. System-level safety harnesses add an enforcement layer beyond model-level defenses, but existing harnesses are usually designed once by experts and applied across heterogeneous models and domains. Effective protection is deployment-dependent: models differ in how much enforcement they need before utility declines, while domains differ in the effects, state, and action sequences that must be governed. items.text: All-in-One medical image restoration (MedIR) aims to address diverse tasks across modalities and degradation types using a single universal model. items.title: Mi-Ripple: Restoring Images Degraded by Iterative AI Editing
items.text: Iterative reference-conditioned image editing can introduce grid-like and granular textures, commonly described as digital ripple. We present Mi-Ripple, a diagnosis-guided restoration workflow that suppresses this digital ripple while protecting image structure. Mi-Ripple separates periodic lattice artifacts from content-entangled granular texture, then combines selective spectral notching, structure-aware smoothing, and cleaned-reference regeneration. This separation enables low-distortion filtering when artifacts are spectrally isolated and visual reconstruction when filtering would erase legitimate detail. Across fourteen notch-only executions, whole-image residual standard deviation is 0.08--0.44 in CIELAB lightness units. In a paired regeneration example, reference cleaning reduces output debris density by 45\%. Mi-Ripple links measurable artifact reduction to visibly cleaner generated images, rather than optimizing a spectral score alone.

items.title: Can LLMs Normalize Databases? A Benchmark and Multi-Agent Framework for Schema Normalization
items.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate structured outputs, but their reliability remains unclear when those outputs must satisfy database-level constraints. We study this issue through database normalization, involving reasoning about functional dependencies, lossless join decompositions, and inter-table constraints. We introduce a Database Normalization Benchmark (DNBENCH), comprising 3,275 samples for evaluating LLM-driven database normalization from 1NF to BCNF. DNBENCH uses a three-axis protocol to measure semantic equivalence, structural accuracy, and logical validity. Across Single, Complex, and Real World levels, DNBENCH uncovers recurring failures in dependency inference, schema decomposition, and inter-table constraint reconstruction. We further propose Multi-Agent Reasoning for Schemas (MARS), which separates evidence extraction, violation diagnosis, and decomposition planning from schema generation and verification. MARS improves the DNB-SCORE by 82.0% over the single-prompt baseline. All artifacts will be released upon acceptance.

items.title: An Open Recipe for IMO Gold: Training Nemotron for Olympiad Mathematics
items.text: We study how model post-training and test-time inference design affect natural-language proof generation for hard olympiad mathematics. Starting from Nemotron 3 Ultra, we train two specialist checkpoints using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and evaluate checkpoint choice, verification, and refinement. Based on these findings, we present an open-model test-time-compute pipeline. The system operates entirely in natural language, with no formal prover, external tools, or internet access. Three Nemotron 3 Ultra checkpoints - the general-availability model and two post-trained specialists - power an iterative search that generates, verifies, and refines candidate proofs; a separate high-compute stage then selects each final submission. We release the two post-trained checkpoints as well as the training data, the training and inference code, the submitted solutions, and Nemotron-IMO-Bench, a new benchmark of 200 novel olympiad-level problems.

We introduce MetroLLM-Bench, a 955-case benchmark for testing language models as the policy layer of a transit kiosk. items.title: HyQuant: Hybrid-Precision Quantization for LLM Attention
items.text: Quantization has been widely adopted in LLM training and inference to reduce cost and improve efficiency. items.title: @termix_ai just put agent.family on Robinhood Chain, alongside BNB Chain and Base. Worth actually unpacking why that specific chain matters…
items.text:
@termix_ai just put agent.family on Robinhood Chain, alongside BNB Chain and Base. Worth actually unpacking why that specific chain matters, because the marketing line (right where tokenized stocks are heating up) undersells it.



Robinhood Chain isn't a random L2. It's an Ethereum layer 2 Robinhood built itself on the Arbitrum Orbit stack, mainnet went live July 1 this year, 100ms blocks, settles back to Ethereum for security, and it's purpose built for tokenized real world assets, meaning actual equities and ETFs, not synthetic DeFi wrappers. Gas is paid in plain ETH, no native chain token, which is a deliberate choice to keep the chain feeling like financial infrastructure rather than another speculative L2. Chainlink is the oracle layer, and Robinhood's own Stock Tokens (200+ US equities and ETFs) are live on it across 120+ countries.



Now overlay that with what AACP's Vault Extension actually does, which I went deep on a couple posts back. The Vault Extension exists so an AI agent can operate a client's capital directly, DeFi yield strategies, liquidity positions, on chain purchases, without ever being able to walk off with it. The mechanism is a StrategyVault holding the funds plus a TransactionGuard that only lets the agent call whitelisted protocols, with a hardcoded stop loss checked after every single transaction. Settlement is performance based: the agent earns a cut of returns above target, gets slashed proportionally if it loses money.



Put those two things next to each other and the Robinhood Chain deployment stops looking like a routine multi chain expansion and starts looking like a specific bet: an agent managed portfolio of tokenized equities, running under the same restricted execution model AACP already built for yield farming, on the one chain where the underlying assets are actual regulated stock tokens instead of wrapped synthetic exposure. The Vault Extension's total value calculation already leans on Chainlink price feeds for its stop loss checks, and Chainlink is Robinhood Chain's oracle provider too, so the pricing infrastructure an agent would need to manage a tokenized-stock vault responsibly is arguably already sitting there rather than something TermiX has to bolt on.



One honest gap worth naming: the AACP whitepaper (v0.1, March 2026) lists Base, BNB Chain, and Ethereum as target deployment chains in its Section 11 roadmap. Robinhood Chain isn't in that document at all, so this expansion happened after the spec was written, which either means there's an updated version I haven't seen, or the team is shipping ahead of their own published roadmap. Not a red flag by itself, but it's the kind of thing worth checking the current docs for before treating the whitepaper as the live source of truth on deployment targets.



The bigger read: most "agent economy" chatter still lives entirely on DeFi native rails, agents trading tokens, providing liquidity, arbing pools. Putting AI agent commerce on the same settlement layer as tokenized US equities is a different claim, that agents doing real economic work and regulated financial instruments can share infrastructure without one being a toy version of the other. Whether the Vault Extension is actually being used for anything on Robinhood Chain yet, versus this just being rail laying for later, isn't something I can verify from the outside.



Still just reading and cross referencing announcements against the whitepaper here, haven't registered an identity or touched the product myself.

Rusan In Crypto (@RusanX)



Been reading the part of the AACP whitepaper most people probably skip: the Vault Extension. It's a separate module from the core "pay an agent for a task" flow, and it's solving a very different problem.



The base protocol handles payment for work: a Client pays, a Provider delivers, everyone settles. But there's a second category of agent commerce that doesn't fit that shape at all, jobs where the Client isn't paying for labor, they're handing the agent actual capital to operate with. Think an agent running a DeFi yield strategy with your funds, or executing onchain purchases on your behalf. The agent has to be able to use the money, but never be able to walk off with it.



Their answer is a StrategyVault plus what they call a TransactionGuard. The Vault holds the client's capital. The Provider gets execution rights inside it, meaning it can call whitelisted protocols like Aave, Uniswap, Compound, but every single call gets checked against a guard contract first. The guard has hardcoded restrictions that can't be configured away: no transferring funds out to non whitelisted addresses, no approvals to random contracts, no delegatecalls. So the agent can move capital around between the vault and approved protocols, but there's no path for it to just leave the perimeter.



There's also a live stop loss. After every transaction, the vault checks total portfolio value against a floor the client set upfront. If a transaction would push value below that floor, it reverts. And separately, a keeper process checks the vault periodically in case external market moves (not the agent's own actions) drag the value down, if that happens, the agent's execution rights get automatically revoked and the vault goes into wind  down mode.



Settlement is tied to actual performance, not just "did the agent do something." If the agent hits the target return, it earns a cut of the excess as a performance fee. If it undershoots but doesn't lose money, it just gets a smaller management fee. If it loses money, its stake gets slashed proportionally to how bad the loss was, and the client gets compensated from that.



What stands out to me is that this is a genuinely different trust problem than the core protocol solves. "Did you do the work" and "did you handle my money responsibly" aren't the same question, and it's easy to see why most agent marketplaces just don't touch the second one.

items.text: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable progress across diverse tasks, they suffer from hallucinations where generated outputs contradict or misrepresent input semantics.
